name: Processor D
justification: Empirical benchmarking of Processor A demonstrates that its tree graph lacks cycles, forcing 7 routing SWAPs (21 extra two-qubit gates) at step count 4 and accelerating depolarizing decoherence. While Processor B contains a 4-cycle that eliminates SWAPs for the 4-qubit ring, its hub node reaches degree 5, which violates planar chip design rules and introduces severe crosstalk and spectator dephasing. Processor D addresses these bottlenecks through a 6-qubit 2x3 ladder architecture with 7 nearest-neighbor edges. This geometry embeds two native 4-cycles (nodes 0-1-4-3 and 1-2-5-4), eliminating 100% of routing SWAPs for the periodic TFIM ring Hamiltonian and tying Processor B's S3 benchmark performance by construction. Crucially, Processor D improves hardware feasibility by strictly capping maximum qubit degree at 3 (versus B's degree 5) and reduces chip diameter to 3. Consequently, the farthest physical pair requires only 2 SWAPs (7 CX gates) compared to 10 CX gates on higher-diameter planar grids. Error rates are fixed to the official baseline model (p1=0.001, p2=0.005, p_readout=0.01) to ensure rigorous and fair comparison. The accepted trade-off is a reduced qubit footprint (6 qubits) tailored specifically to 1D and quasi-1D quantum simulations.
